title: Massachusetts Rent Increase Laws: Know Your Rights
summary: Massachusetts banned rent control in 1994, and a 2026 ballot question to bring it back was struck down in June. Here's what actually limits a rent increase in Massachusetts today.
body_markdown:
Massachusetts is one of the most expensive rental markets in the country, and it is also one where the law puts no ceiling on what your landlord can charge. That combination catches a lot of renters off guard at renewal time.


What Massachusetts does give you is process: written notice, protection from mid-lease increases, and unusually strict rules about your security deposit.


Here's what applies today, including where the rent control debate currently stands.


Here's what we'll cover:


- How Much Can a Landlord Raise Rent in Massachusetts?
- What Happened to Rent Control in Massachusetts
- Massachusetts Rent Increase Laws
- How To Tell if a Rent Increase Is Legal
- How To Negotiate a Lower Rent in Massachusetts
- Final Thoughts


## How Much Can a Landlord Raise Rent in Massachusetts?


There is no legal cap. Massachusetts has no statewide rent control, and no city or town in Massachusetts currently has rent control either — not Boston, not Cambridge, not Brookline.


A landlord can raise the rent by any amount, as long as they give proper written notice and aren't doing it for a prohibited reason.


## What Happened to Rent Control in Massachusetts


This comes up constantly, and the history explains why the answer is "no cap" in a state people assume has one.


Rent control existed in Boston, Brookline, and Cambridge until 1994. That November, a statewide ballot measure known as Question 9 abolished it. The measure passed narrowly — about 51% to 49% — and notably, **all three cities that actually had rent control voted against it.** They were outvoted by the rest of the state. You can read more of that history in[this overview of rent control in Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rent_control_in_Massachusetts) .


It has been banned ever since.


### The 2026 ballot question


Tenant advocates tried to bring it back. A group called Homes for All Massachusetts gathered enough signatures to put a rent stabilization measure on the November 2026 ballot. It would have capped annual rent increases at 5%, with exemptions for owner-occupied buildings of four units or fewer and for newly built housing in its first ten years.


**It will not appear on the ballot.** On June 23, 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court[struck the question](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/06/23/massachusetts-high-court-rent-control-ballot-question-struck) , ruling that because the petition included a religious exemption it "relates to religion, religious practices or religious institutions" — a subject the state constitution bars from the initiative process. Attorney General Andrea Campbell acknowledged the state had erred in certifying it.


Advocates have said they'll pursue rent stabilization through the legislature instead. For now, nothing has changed: there is no cap on rent increases in Massachusetts. ([Further background on the ruling.](https://www.gtlaw.com/en/insights/2026/6/massachusetts-high-court-takes-rent-control-initiative-off-2026-ballot) )


## Massachusetts Rent Increase Laws


### Notice Period


Your landlord must give you at least **30 days written notice, or one full rental period — whichever is longer** — before a rent increase takes effect. The notice has to state the new amount and the date it starts.


"One full rental period" matters if your rent is due on a schedule other than monthly. For a standard month-to-month tenancy, notice given partway through a month generally doesn't take effect until the month after next.


### Your Landlord Can't Raise Rent Mid-Lease


If you have a fixed-term lease, the rent is locked for the term. An increase can only take effect at renewal, or after proper notice if you're a tenant at will (month-to-month with no written lease).


Tenants at will have less protection here — but they still get the full notice period, and a rent increase is effectively an offer to change the tenancy that you can decline.


### Security Deposits Are Strictly Regulated


Massachusetts has some of the strictest deposit rules in the country, and they're worth knowing because they don't move when the rent does.


- A security deposit **cannot exceed one month's rent** , full stop. This doesn't scale up with a rent increase the way it can in some states.
- The deposit must be held in a separate, interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and you're entitled to a receipt identifying the bank and account.
- You're owed **interest** on the deposit annually.
- At move-in your landlord must give you a statement of the unit's condition.


Landlords who don't follow these rules can face significant penalties. If your landlord raises the rent and asks for a deposit top-up that would exceed one month's rent, that request isn't allowed.


### When an Increase Isn't Legal


- **Retaliation.** Massachusetts protects tenants who report code violations, request repairs, or organize. An increase that arrives soon after you exercised one of those rights may be presumed retaliatory. Document the dates.
- **Discrimination.** State and federal fair housing law prohibit increases based on protected characteristics. Massachusetts protections are broader than the federal baseline and include, among others, source of income — meaning a landlord can't raise your rent because you use a housing voucher.
- **Mid-lease increases** , unless your lease provides for them.


## How To Tell if a Rent Increase Is Legal


1. **Are you inside a fixed lease term?** If so, the increase waits for renewal.
2. **Was the notice in writing, and did it give you 30 days or one full rental period, whichever is longer?**
3. **Does it name the new amount and the start date?**
4. **Is your deposit still at or below one month's rent?** It can't go above that.
5. **What happened just before the notice arrived?** If you'd reported a problem, note the sequence.


Put any dispute in writing and keep copies. Massachusetts tenants have real remedies, but they depend on a paper trail.


## How To Negotiate a Lower Rent in Massachusetts


With no cap in place, negotiation is the main lever you have.


### Time it to the market


Massachusetts rental demand is heavily seasonal, especially around the September 1 turnover in the Boston area. A landlord facing a vacancy in a slow month has far more reason to negotiate than one who can re-list into peak season. If your renewal lands off-peak, say so.


### Bring comparable listings


Concrete numbers beat a general objection. Pull three or four genuinely comparable units nearby and their current asking rents. If your increase puts you above that range, you have a specific case to make.


### Offer term instead of money


A longer lease is worth real money to a landlord — it removes a turnover and the weeks of vacancy that come with it. Trading a two-year commitment for a smaller increase is a common landing spot.


### Make yourself cheap to keep


Turnover costs a landlord cleaning, repairs, listing fees, and lost rent. A tenant who pays on time and looks after the place is worth keeping, and it's reasonable to point that out during a renewal conversation.


Renters insurance is a small part of that. Massachusetts doesn't require it, but plenty of leases do, and it shows a landlord you're covered if something goes wrong. It also covers you — your landlord's policy insures the building, not your belongings, and not your liability if someone is injured in your apartment.

You can also compare options in our guide to the[best renters insurance in Massachusetts](https://www.goodcover.com/blog/best-renters-insurance-massachusetts) .


## Final Thoughts: Massachusetts Rent Increase Laws


Massachusetts has no rent cap, hasn't had one since 1994, and won't get one from the 2026 ballot. What you do have is a real notice requirement, a firm rule against mid-lease increases, and the strictest security deposit rules in the country.


Those are the parts worth checking when an increase arrives — and the deposit rules in particular are where landlords most often get it wrong.
